forecasts.question: Will Labour be largest party at next UK General Election?
forecasts.key_change: Down 1pp to 2%. May 7 locals are confirming a category-rare collapse: in the first three councils to declare on May 8, Labour lost 26 seats while Reform gained 34. Hartlepool: Reform won 12 of 12. Halton: Reform won 15 of 17. Redditch: Reform won 8 of 9. YouGov 4-5 May voting intention has Reform 25%, Labour 18%, Con 17%, Green 15%, LD 14% — a genuinely fragmented field where Labour is no longer the natural challenger. Electoral Calculus April MRP projects a Reform+Con coalition with Farage as PM. For Labour to be largest party, the electorate would need to shift back ~7-9pp net to Labour from Reform/Greens AND the fragmentation to favour Labour's vote efficiency — neither is consistent with current trajectory.
forecasts.base_rate: Sitting government re-elected as largest party ~50% historically; but UK has not had a one-term majority government become non-largest since 1979 — shifts this baseline materially
factors_up: Time to election: up to 3.5 years for Labour to recover (+2pp)
Fragmentation could split the right vote (Reform vs Con) and benefit Labour seat-efficiency (+1pp)
FPTP punishes dispersed vote — even ~25-28% Labour share could yield largest party in unusual scenarios (+1pp)
factors_down: Labour at 18% in latest YouGov — historic low (-3pp)
Reform-Con combined polling ~42% with right-vote consolidation possible (-2pp)
Local election losses on May 7 deeper than worst pre-election expectations (-2pp)
Electoral Calculus MRP central case is Reform+Con coalition with Farage PM (-1pp)
key_uncertainties: Whether Starmer is replaced and whether a leadership change rebuilds Labour brand
Whether Reform fades or consolidates in 2027-28 (party history of regression)
Whether the Greens take Labour-vulnerable urban seats, suppressing Labour vote efficiency

update_triggers.up: Sustained Labour polling recovery to mid-20s; Reform internal split or scandal reversing momentum
update_triggers.down: Labour polls drop below 15%; Reform-Con vote management deal emerges before election

forecasts.key_change: Down 1pp to 8%. The Iran/Strait of Hormuz precedent is being studied but not adopted. With ~44 months remaining and demonstrable expert consensus that the pre-2027 window is closing without action, the probability of resolving YES drifts down.

forecasts.question: Will UK annual CPI inflation fall below 2.0% for at least one month before 1 January 2027?
forecasts.key_change: Hold at 1%. March 2026 CPI ran at 3.3% (up from 3.0% in February); the April 2026 release on May 20 will likely show further sticky services inflation. With only 8 monthly releases remaining (April through November 2026 published before 1 Jan 2027), CPI would need a ~1.4pp drop in a single step — historically rare absent a sharp deflationary shock. Bank of England April 2026 MPR continues to anchor inflation above target into 2027. Effectively requires recession-grade demand collapse or a one-off energy base-effect collapse.

factors_up: Energy base effects could compress headline CPI in summer 2026 (+1pp)

BoE projects CPI above 2% target through 2027 (-1pp)
key_uncertainties: Whether a sharp energy correction in H2 2026 produces a base-effect-led <2% print

forecasts.question: Will UK average annual real GDP growth exceed 1.5% across the 2030s (2030-2039)?
forecasts.key_change: Down 1pp to 41%. OBR March 2026 EFO continues to anchor 1.1% in 2026 and 1.6% in 2027. IFS expects ~1.4% from 2026 onwards. May 7 local-election results materially confirm the Reform-leaning political trajectory: Reform gaining 30+ seats in first three councils declared, Labour losing 25+. A Reform-led or Reform-Con government would likely produce more aggressive deregulation (planning, AI uptake) but also lower migration, harder EU trade rules, and fiscal volatility — net direction on 2030s GDP is genuinely two-sided. Productivity assumptions and labour-supply outlook remain the cruxes; demographic ageing continues to drag.
